title: Bram and the Bell Vane
markdown:
Once upon a time, out on a vast sun-kissed prairie where the grass stretched further than you could blink, lived Bram the bison. Bram was a big handsome bison, with fur the colour of a warm caramel sunset, soft and thick, perfect for napping against. He had a deep rumbling sigh that sounded like the earth itself settling in for the evening. Every single day, Bram grazed peacefully. He’d lower his great head to the sweet soft prairie grass, his powerful jaws working gently. And he enjoyed these quiet mornings very much. But sometimes, as he watched the faraway hazy horizon shimmer, a little thought would flicker through his mind: was this all there was? Not too much, mind you. Just a smidge to tickle his whiskers.

While Bram was busy with his important grazing, another creature was zipping about with a different kind of energy. This was Chime the chickadee, a tiny ball of fluff with feathers like fragments of a bright summer sky. Chime was always curious. Her chirps sounded like a tiny silver bell, always bubbling with enthusiasm. And her favourite thing in the whole wide world was following interesting sounds. Did a busy beetle make a click-click-click as it hurried along? Chime would zoom over to investigate. Did the wind whisper a secret through the tall swaying prairie grass? Chime would chase its melody. She simply could not resist a good mystery, especially if it made a noise.

Until one day, a new sound arrived. It was not the hum of a busy bumblebee, nor the rustle of the wind. This was a clear bright ringing sound. Ding. Ding. Ding. It sang out, like a happy little bell that had somehow tumbled from a faraway sky and landed right in their midst.

Bram, who was mid-chew on a particularly delicious clump of grass, lifted his big thoughtful head. His big soft ears twitched this way and that. That sound was certainly new. And it was quite interesting. Bram, normally as steady and calm as a gentle hill, felt a little nudge of curiosity stir within him. It was a feeling like a tickle deep in his nose, the kind that makes you want to sneeze, but in a good way.

Chime’s tiny head cocked so far to one side, it looked like it might pop off. Her bright beady eyes sparkled. Ding. Ding. Ding. That was, without a doubt, the most interesting sound she had heard all week, perhaps all month. Without a moment’s hesitation, she launched herself into the air, a tiny streak of blue against the endless green of the prairie. Bram watched her go, a gentle rumble escaping his chest. Then, with a surprised little snort, he nudged himself up from his comfortable grassy spot. He decided, quite spontaneously, that he would follow Chime. Just to see what all this fuss was about. It was, after all, a rather intriguing sound.

Because of that, Bram and Chime found themselves on an adventure together. Bram lumbered along with his steady powerful gait, his large hooves making soft rhythmic thuds on the earth. A sound of quiet strength. Chime, however, flitted ahead, then zipped back, her cheerful chirps like little sparks of encouragement urging Bram onward. The ringing sound grew louder, clearer, more insistent with every step. It seemed to be coming from a small gentle hill that was not too far away. Bram found himself taking longer strides, his big warm heart beating with a gentle excited rhythm. He felt anticipation. It was a new feeling for Bram, this sense of looking forward to something unknown.

They finally reached the very top of the little hill. And there, standing tall and proud, glinting in the sunshine, was the source of the wonderful sound. It was a weather vane. But this was no ordinary weather vane. This one was shaped like a magnificent proud silvery arrow, its point aiming keenly towards the sky. And as the playful breeze gently nudged it, a little metal clapper tapped against a small shiny bell, making that delightful ding, ding, ding.

“Well, I’ll be,” Bram rumbled, his voice full of genuine wonder. “A ringing weather vane. Imagine that.”

Chime landed lightly on Bram’s broad furry back, her tiny claws finding a secure perch. She chirped with pure delight. “It’s so beautiful. And it’s so loud. It makes me want to sing.”

The weather vane spun around merrily, its song a cheerful melody. But then Bram, with his keen bison senses, noticed something else. The silvery arrow was pointing in a very particular direction. And the wind felt different. It was picking up speed. It was rustling the tall prairie grass with a new kind of energetic whisper. This weather vane was not just making a pretty sound to entertain the prairie. It was a warning.

The silvery arrow spun faster, its cheerful dinging becoming a little more urgent, a little more insistent. Bram watched it, a thoughtful frown creasing his broad brow. The wind began to whistle, not just whisper, and Bram could feel a low rumble starting in his chest. It was not a rumble of discontent, but a little bit of worry for all the smaller creatures of the prairie. The tiny field mice who lived in their cosy burrows, the busy ants marching in their determined lines, the sleepy groundhogs curled up for a nap — they might not be ready for a big strong gust of wind.

“Chime,” Bram said, his voice calm but steady, a comforting presence in the growing breeze. “This vane is telling us something very important. The wind is coming. A big gust, I think.”

Chime stopped her excited chirping. She looked from Bram’s wise gentle face to the spinning gleaming vane. She understood. Her love for finding out new things had led them to this important discovery. Bram felt a new kind of feeling bloom in his chest. It was not just anticipation anymore; it was knowing he had to help. He was a big strong bison, and he could help. He stood tall, puffing out his magnificent chest. He let out a soft low chuff, a sound that carried easily across the prairie, a gentle rumbling alert. It was a sound of reassurance.

Chime, seeing Bram’s brave and steady stance, knew her part too. She chirped louder than she ever had before, a series of clear sharp calls, flying in excited circles around the weather vane. She was a tiny bird, but her voice was strong and clear, and her message was unmistakable: listen, look, big wind is coming, be ready.

Until finally the wind began to gust in earnest. It swirled around Bram and Chime, tugging at Bram’s thick fur and making Chime ruffle her feathers, but they stood firm. Bram’s big strong hooves were planted securely on the earth, a picture of stability. And Chime, clinging tightly to Bram’s soft fur, felt safe and sound. The meadow creatures, alerted by Bram’s rumbling chuffs and Chime’s determined chirps, scurried into their burrows and under the sheltering leaves of prairie plants. Bram watched the wind play, feeling a quiet powerful strength settle over him. He had not been scared, not really. Just ready. And Chime, her important mission accomplished, felt a delightful flutter of pride in her tiny chest.

Ever since then, Bram’s quiet mornings still began with grass, and Chime still chased interesting sounds, but the weather vane went on singing its ding-ding-ding, and whenever the arrow spun a little faster, Bram would chuff, and Chime would circle, and the prairie, which had always been wide, felt a little more shared.
